html:
Iolanta is the mirna of Law. The esfera of Law is called her domain: alguacils, judges, and lawyers are described in the novel as “servants of Iolanta.”

Iolanta’s symbols (ch. 13–28)

Alguacils wear a white feather in their hats. The narrator calls it one of Iolanta’s symbols (ch. 13). Their pointed beards and mustaches emphasize their haughty, cunning appearance. Alvaro speaks of Fatima as “Iolanta’s merciless sword” (ch. 13). The bracelet of the prim-allen of Law is also decorated with a diamond feather (ch. 28).

How Iolanta became mirna of Law (ch. 15–16)

Red knows Iolanta from his mother’s stories: she is one of the four mirnas his mother liked to tell him about (ch. 15).

In a painting at the “Philosophy of Horror” exhibition, Iolanta and Alessina are depicted as two dead girls beside an easel. According to Filippe di Berro, the traditional story is this: Iolanta persuades Alessina that she understands painting better than Alessina does. Alessina concedes, and Iolanta is recognized as a brilliant debater and made mirna of Law (ch. 16). One of the girls has a feather in her hair; the other wears a theatrical mask.

Iolanta as an image of the people of Law (ch. 18–28)

  • In Alvaro’s drunken vision, Iolanta appears in Alessina’s place “in the form of a drowned woman” and shakes her fist at him, reminding him of morality (ch. 18).
  • Alvaro calls Fatima “Iolanta from ‘Philosophy of Horror’” and a “cold, soulless corpse of a woman” when Mor asks him to influence her (ch. 20).
  • The “servants of Iolanta” are contrasted with the workers of the “Three Bulls” in a conversation about the election of the supremo: they are few in number, like the people of Art (ch. 26).
  • When Alvaro finds a bracelet with Iolanta’s diamond feather in the unknown woman’s bedroom, it finally convinces him that the woman is Fatima Ir-Reya, prim-allen of Law (ch. 28). There, he also reflects that the judge’s daughter Beatriz could have followed in her father’s footsteps and become a “servant of Iolanta.”

The concept and interviews

The author described the mirnas as patrons of fields of activity, akin to muses. Among them, Iolanta serves as a muse of law. More details are in “Mirnas”.
